title: Two minutes on the analyst's desk
spec: M27 · escalation briefs, approval gates, decision injection
intro: The same borderline debtor, handed to a human three ways: decided silently, dumped as a 12-step log, and packaged as a one-page brief. Only one of the three gives the reviewer a verdict they can actually stand behind.

provenance.source: a narrated escalation on one borderline UCC debtor; token counts, confidence scores, and review times are plausible inventions, not measurements

foot: The discipline here is M27's escalation brief — decision, recommendation with confidence, why, scoped evidence with provenance, options — and the return leg that injects the human's call back into agent state.

steps.title: Confidence 0.55, and nobody was asked
narrative: The agent scores ACME LOGISTICS & DISTRIBUTION, L.L.C. It finds two active liens, one termination that was filed but not yet reflected, and a name that nearly matches a second entity. The signals conflict, and the score comes back at 0.55 confidence — the agent's own way of saying it is barely more sure than a coin.

It writes risk: HIGH anyway and returns. No flag, no pause, no reviewer. A credit committee reads HIGH four days later and declines a $2M facility on it. The first human to see the reasoning is the one writing the complaint response.
steps.claudeSays: I recorded a confidence of 0.55 and then acted as if it were 0.95. Nothing in the loop treated that number as a trigger.
steps.youDo: Find the confidence score in your own agent's output and check what, if anything, branches on it. In most pipelines the answer is nothing.

before.title: WHAT WAS WRITTEN TO THE DECISION STORE

steps.title: The fix that makes it worse — send everything
narrative: So you add an escalation. When confidence drops below 0.70, stop and hand it to an analyst. The implementation is the obvious one: attach the agent's context so nothing is hidden. That is 18,400 tokens — twelve reasoning steps, four raw tool results, thirty filing records, the retrieval scores.

The analyst opens it, scrolls for six minutes, and never finds the pending termination: it is one line inside the fourth tool result. Faced with a wall and a queue, they do what everyone does with a wall and a queue. They approve it.
A rubber stamp is not a review. Worse, it now looks like one in the audit trail — a human name against a decision no human understood.
steps.claudeSays: I gave the analyst complete information and no decision. Completeness is not the same as sufficiency.

steps.title: The brief — five fields, 340 tokens
narrative: Replace the log with a brief. Five fields, in this order: the decision being asked for, the recommendation and its confidence, the why in two lines, the evidence — three filings, each with its ID so the analyst can open it — and the options they may choose between.

It is 340 tokens. Everything the agent knows is still on disk; what changed is that the analyst is handed the decision instead of the derivation. The pending termination is now the second line of the brief rather than line 900 of a tool result.
The analyst reads it, opens filing 0019988 to confirm the termination is real, and calls MEDIUM in forty seconds. That is a review you can defend.
steps.youDo: Write escalation_brief(state) as a function that returns exactly those five fields and nothing else. If it can reach a field, that is not a reason to include it.

steps.title: The return leg — inject the decision, or it never happened
narrative: A handoff has two directions and most implementations build one. The analyst's call comes back as a chat message, someone pastes the grade into a ticket, and the agent — still holding its own 0.55 reasoning — resumes, re-derives HIGH on the next step, and quietly contradicts the human who was just asked.

Close it properly. The decision re-enters agent state in the operator tier: authoritative, above the agent's own inference, carrying the analyst's rationale as new knowledge the agent did not have. 0044120 is a different entity is now a fact in the run, not an open question.

Then log it. Who decided, what they saw, what they chose, and why — keyed to the brief they were shown. That last part matters: an audit entry that records a decision but not the evidence in front of the decider proves nothing later.
steps.claudeSays: The grade is now MEDIUM because an authorized human set it, not because I inferred it. My 0.55 is still in the record as the reason I asked.
steps.youDo: After your approval step, assert that the agent's next action reads the human's value and not its own — a one-line check that catches the one-way handoff before production does.

views.text: Three things had to be true for this to be a real approval: the trigger fired on a number the agent already knew, the human was handed a decision rather than a derivation, and their answer came back as authoritative state instead of a chat message. Drop any one and you have a gate that only looks like one.
